summary: The GRE Key field can identify a particular data stream. This standards-track document defines a Mobile IPv4 extension for exchanging the value to use in that field. Mobility agents can also prepare their interfaces before traffic starts.

plainLanguage.summary: A tunnel can have a label on each stream. This lets mobile network parts agree on the label ahead of time.

questions: how is gre key negotiated in mobile ip
what is the gre key extension in mobile ipv4
what is mobile ipv4 extension type 48
why use gre instead of ip-in-ip in mobile ip
subtitle: A Mobile IPv4 extension that lets a Foreign Agent and Home Agent agree on the GRE key that labels each tunneled data stream.

tldr.problem: When many subscriber sessions share the same care-of address, home address and Home Agent address, IP-in-IP tunneling cannot tell their data streams apart. A Foreign Agent also needs a way to ask for GRE tunneling without changing Home Agent behavior.
tldr.mechanism: A new non-skippable Mobile IPv4 extension (type 48) carries a four-octet GRE key in Registration Requests and Replies. Each side then puts the key it was given into the GRE Key field of the packets it sends.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run home networks made of several VPNs with overlapping home addresses, because the GRE key identifies each session's stream. The word key here means an index, not a secret.

today: RFC 6245 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a GRE Key for Mobile IPv4
sections.content:
RFC 6245 defines a new extension for a Foreign Agent (FA) running Mobile IP for IPv4. The extension lets the FA request Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) tunneling without disturbing the Home Agent (HA) behavior specified for Mobile IPv4 in RFC 5944. The extension carries the GRE key from RFC 2890 that is needed to set up a GRE tunnel between the FA and the HA.

The motivation is operator networks whose home networks consist of multiple Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) that may have overlapping home addresses. If the tuple of Care of Address, Home Address and Home Agent Address is the same across several subscriber sessions, the FA and HA can use the GRE key to tell the sessions' data streams apart. With plain IP-in-IP tunneling the streams cannot be distinguished, which the RFC calls a significant drawback.
sections.plainLanguage: Many kids share one tunnel and have the same address. A number sticker on each parcel tells the helpers whose parcel is whose.

sections.title: Foreign Agent Behavior
sections.content:
The FA MUST support IP-in-IP tunneling for Mobile IPv4. It may also support GRE tunneling, for example to allow overlapping private home addresses. An FA that can do GRE should set the G bit in the Flags field of the Agent Advertisement it sends to the Mobile Node (MN). An FA that cannot do GRE MUST reset that bit, and if the MN then sets G in its Registration Request, the FA answers with the code 'requested encapsulation unavailable' (72).

If the MN sets neither the G bit nor the D bit (decapsulation by the mobile node, used with a co-located care-of address), and local policy lets the FA override, the FA MUST include the GRE Key Extension in the Registration Request it passes to the HA. The presence of the extension is a request for GRE encapsulation and takes precedence over the G bit. The FA MUST NOT change the G bit itself, because it is protected by the Mobile-Home Authentication extension.

When GRE is used and the D bit is not set, the FA MUST include a GRE key in all Registration Requests: initial, renewal and de-registration. It may send a key of value zero to signal that the HA assigns GRE keys in both directions. How keys are assigned is outside the scope of the memo. The extension goes after any MN-HA and MN-FA Challenge and MN-AAA extensions and before any FA-HA Auth extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The foreign helper says whether it can use number stickers. If the traveler did not ask for stickers but the helper wants them, the helper adds a note to the request without touching the traveler's signed paperwork.

sections.title: Home Agent and Mobile Node Behavior
sections.content:
The HA MUST process the extension in Registration Requests following RFC 5944. The extension is non-skippable, so an HA that does not recognize it MUST silently discard the message and use other forms of encapsulation, such as IP-in-IP, when the mobile node asks for them. An HA that recognizes the extension but is not configured for GRE MUST send a Registration Reply (RRP) with code 'requested encapsulation unavailable (139)' from RFC 3024.

If a Registration Request carries the extension but not the G bit, the HA SHOULD behave as though G were set. When the HA supports GRE, it SHOULD accept the request with code 'registration accepted (0)', MUST assign a GRE key and MUST include the extension in the reply, and in every reply to a request that included it, when a key is available.

If the initial request carries a key of zero, the HA SHOULD accept it, MUST assign keys for both directions and MUST return them in the extension. An MN that is capable of GRE encapsulation SHOULD set the G bit in its Registration Request.
sections.plainLanguage: The home helper either understands the sticker note and replies with its own sticker number, or it says it cannot do stickers. If it has never heard of stickers, it ignores the request and the old way is used.

sections.title: The GRE Key Extension Format
sections.content:
Once keys are exchanged, GRE keying is allowed to be asymmetric. The FA assigns a key for traffic it will receive and the HA may assign its own. The FA then uses the HA-assigned key in the GRE header for reverse tunneling, and the HA uses the FA-assigned key. The extension MAY appear in Registration Requests or Replies and tells the recipient which value to place in the GRE Key field.

The extension has four fields: an 8-bit Type of 48 (non-skippable), a Sub-Type of 0, a Length of 4, and a four-octet Key Identifier. The key is assigned during registration and inserted in every GRE packet of the user traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a label saying what kind of note it is, a size, and then the sticker number itself. Each side uses the other side's number on parcels it sends.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned Type value 48 for this extension from the non-skippable range (0-127) of Mobile IP extensions. The extension also creates a new sub-type numbering space, in which value 0 is assigned from the range 0 to 255. New sub-type values are approved through Expert Review with Specification Required.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of note types got a new entry, number 48, and a new small list for sub-kinds where only the first slot is used so far.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 5944. The RFC adds that, despite its name, the GRE Key Extension has little to do with security. Here the word key is an index or demultiplexing value used to tell packets of one flow from another within a GRE tunnel. It is not a cryptographic shared secret to be protected.
sections.plainLanguage: The number sticker is just a label to sort parcels. It is not a secret password.

fields.name: Key Identifier
fields.desc: Four-octet value assigned during registration and inserted in every GRE packet of the user traffic.
